a man takes ibuprofen because it makes his headache go away, and he becomes more likely to take ibuprofen in the future. this is: positive reinforcement negative reinforcement positive punishment negative punishment
which reinforcement schedule produces behavior that is most resistant to extinction? fixed ratio fixed interval variable ratio continuous

a parent praises a child after she finishes her homework, and she does homework more often. which change would turn this into an example of negative reinforcement? letting her skip a disliked chore when she finishes homework taking away her video games whenever she skips her homework adding an extra chore to her list when she skips her homework giving her a sticker each time she finishes her homework

participants see lists of letters on a screen and recall them in order. lists of similar sounding letters (b, d, g, p, t) are recalled worse than dissimilar ones (f, k, q, r, x). when participants must repeat 'the, the, the' aloud while viewing, the difference disappears. what does this suggest? seen letters are recoded into sound in verbal working memory seen letters are held only as images in visual sensory memory repeating a word aloud improves recall of similar sounding letters letter recall depends mainly on how well each letter is stored in long term memory

in the sea slug aplysia, gentle touches to the siphon cause the gill to withdraw, but the response weakens with repetition. recordings show the sensory neurons still fire to each touch. what most likely causes the weakening? sensory neurons release less transmitter onto motor neurons touch receptors on the siphon stop responding to repeated touches the gill muscle becomes fatigued and can no longer contract fully new synapses form between the sensory neurons and the motor neurons

lab reared monkeys that have never seen a snake watch videos of other monkeys reacting with fear. some watch fear directed at a toy snake; others watch edited videos showing the same fear directed at flowers. only the first group comes to fear the object. what does this suggest? observational learning is constrained by biological preparedness monkeys cannot learn fear simply by watching other monkeys react fear of snakes is inborn and appears without any experience at all the flower videos were less vivid, so those monkeys paid no attention

adults who studied spanish in school were tested years later (hypothetical data: percent of original vocabulary score retained). years since course 0 3 6 25 50 retained (%) 100 60 58 57 55 what does this pattern suggest about long term memory? after early loss, what remains can last for decades memories decay at a steady rate until nothing is left most forgetting happens between 25 and 50 years later long term memory can hold only a few years of material

a doctor hides a pin in his hand and pricks a patient with severe amnesia when they shake hands. minutes later, she cannot recall meeting him, yet she refuses to shake his hand again and can't explain why. what does this show? she lacks an explicit memory of the event but retains an implicit one her explicit memory of the event is intact, but she cannot put it into words she has retrograde amnesia, so she cannot recall events before her injury her refusal reflects a lucky guess, since no memory of the event remains
knowing how to ride a bike is an example of: procedural (implicit) memory episodic (explicit) memory semantic (explicit) memory flashbulb memory

in classical conditioning, extinction occurs when: the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus a previously weakened conditioned response reappears after a rest period the conditioned response spreads to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus the conditioned stimulus is paired with a new, stronger unconditioned stimulus

a child loves video games but dislikes reading. his parents allow 30 minutes of gaming only after he reads for 30 minutes, and his reading time increases. which principle explains this? the premack principle stimulus generalization classical conditioning latent learning
a child bitten by one dog becomes afraid of all dogs. this is: stimulus generalization stimulus discrimination extinction spontaneous recovery

positive punishment is best illustrated by: getting a speeding ticket after driving too fast losing phone privileges for breaking curfew receiving praise from a supervisor for good work taking aspirin to remove a headache

shaping is: reinforcing successive approximations of a desired behavior reinforcing a behavior only after a fixed number of responses pairing a neutral stimulus with one that triggers a reflex learning a behavior by observing and imitating a model

organizing information into meaningful groups (for example, remembering 1 800 555 0199 in chunks) improves: the effective capacity of short term memory the duration of visual sensory (iconic) memory procedural memory for motor skills implicit memory through priming
a student remembers material best when tested in the same room where they studied. this shows: context dependent memory state dependent memory only retroactive interference the serial position effect
a patient can't form new long term memories after surgery but remembers childhood well. this is: anterograde amnesia retrograde amnesia infantile amnesia source amnesia
studying a little each day over two weeks leads to better retention than cramming the night before. this is the: spacing effect serial position effect misinformation effect primacy effect

people remember more words when they think about each word's meaning than when they count its letters. this supports: levels of processing: deeper, semantic encoding aids recall decay theory: unused memory traces fade over time encoding specificity: matching study and test contexts aids retrieval chunking: grouping items expands short term capacity

long term potentiation (ltp) is thought to underlie learning because it: strengthens synapses that are repeatedly activated together weakens synapses that are rarely activated together increases the number of neurons in the hippocampus speeds signal conduction by adding myelin to the most active axons

eyewitnesses who heard the word 'smashed' estimated higher car speeds than those who heard 'hit'. this illustrates: the misinformation effect proactive interference state dependent memory flashbulb memory

a dog salivates to a bell, but not to a buzzer, after learning that only the bell predicts food. later the dog salivates to a light that was repeatedly paired with the bell (never with food). which phenomenon explains the light? second order (higher order) conditioning stimulus generalization to similar cues spontaneous recovery of the response stimulus discrimination between cues

the graph shows recall by list position right after studying. why are the first words recalled well? they were rehearsed more and reached long term memory they were still held in sensory memory at the time of the test they were most recently heard they were shown in a larger font

if recall were tested after a 30 second distraction task, which part of the curve would change most? the right end (recency effect) would drop the left end (primacy effect) would drop the middle would rise sharply the whole curve would rise

the forgetting curve shown is typical for newly learned material. when is the most information lost? in the first hour or so after learning after about one week, once the material is no longer reviewed after about one month forgetting is steady over time

in the conditioning graph shown, responding falls steadily across trials 5 9. what procedure most likely produced this decline? the cs was presented repeatedly without the us the us was presented repeatedly without the cs the cs and us continued to be paired every trial the animal was given a rest period between trials

the graph shows cumulative responses under two reinforcement schedules. schedule 2 shows a 'scallop' pattern, with responding speeding up just before each reward every 10 minutes. which schedule is schedule 2? fixed interval variable ratio variable interval continuous reinforcement

a cat is placed repeatedly in a puzzle box that opens when it pulls a loop. its escape times are shown. trial 1 5 10 20 escape time (s) 160 90 50 15 what does this gradual decline best support? responses that led to escape were strengthened gradually the cat suddenly understood the solution after a period of thought the cat learned by watching other cats escape from the same box escape was an unlearned reflex that was present from the first trial

participants see a row of letters and also hear a list of letters. two seconds later, a cue tells them which part to report. partial reports are accurate for the heard letters but not for the seen letters. what best explains this? echoic memory lasts several seconds; iconic memory fades in under 1 second iconic memory lasts several seconds; echoic memory fades in under 1 second both sensory stores last 2 seconds, but sounds are easier to rehearse heard letters go straight to long term memory, skipping sensory memory

a young man whose hippocampi were damaged at birth cannot remember what he did yesterday or where he put things. yet he went through regular school, learned to read and has a normal vocabulary and knowledge of facts. what does this suggest? episodic memory can be impaired more than semantic memory semantic memory can be impaired more than episodic memory procedural memory is impaired, so he cannot learn new skills his long term memory is intact, but his sensory memory has failed

a medical student who learned spanish in high school is now studying italian. she keeps recalling spanish words when she tries to remember new italian vocabulary. this is: proactive interference retroactive interference anterograde amnesia decay of sensory memory

in sperling's experiments, a 3 × 4 grid of letters flashed for a fraction of a second. participants could report only about 4 or 5 letters in total, but when a tone right after the flash signaled which row to report, they could report most letters in any row. this shows that iconic memory: briefly holds most of the display but fades within a second holds only about four items, like short term memory lasts several minutes if attention is paid to it stores the letters by their sound rather than by their appearance

rats explored a maze for days with no food reward and showed little improvement. once food was placed in the goal box, they quickly ran the maze as well as rats that had been rewarded all along. tolman called this: latent learning shaping spontaneous recovery instinctive drift

an infant stops looking at a picture of a red circle after seeing it many times, but looks for a long time again when a blue square appears. the renewed looking is called: dishabituation sensitization spontaneous recovery stimulus generalization
a factory worker is paid $5 for every 10 garments she finishes. which reinforcement schedule is this? fixed ratio fixed interval variable ratio variable interval

after living through an earthquake, a woman now startles strongly at minor noises, such as a door closing, that never bothered her before. this is: sensitization habituation extinction latent learning
a teenager comes home after curfew, so his parents take away his car keys for a week, and he stops coming home late. this is: negative punishment negative reinforcement positive punishment extinction

a patient with migraines learns that taking medication at the first sign of a visual aura prevents the headache from developing at all. her medication taking is best described as: avoidance learning escape learning positive reinforcement positive punishment

a student who drank coffee while studying recalls more on the exam when she has also had coffee beforehand. this best illustrates: state dependent memory context dependent memory proactive interference the spacing effect

two groups study a science passage for the same total time. group 1 rereads it three times; group 2 reads it once and then takes two practice recall tests. a week later, group 2 remembers more. this illustrates: the testing effect (retrieval practice) the spacing effect (distributed study) the serial position effect the misinformation effect

in watson and rayner's 'little albert' study, a steel bar was struck loudly behind an infant whenever he reached for a white rat. before any pairing, the infant's crying at the loud noise was the: unconditioned response conditioned response unconditioned stimulus conditioned stimulus

children watched a film of an adult hitting a bobo doll. in one version the adult was punished, and those children later imitated less aggression. when all children were then offered treats for copying the adult, the differences between groups largely disappeared. what does this show? children learned the behavior even when they did not perform it punishing the model kept the children from learning anything imitation requires direct reinforcement of the child's own acts observational learning occurs only for nonaggressive acts

participants hear a list: bed, rest, awake, tired, dream, snooze, blanket. many later confidently 'remember' hearing the word sleep, which was never presented. this finding shows that: memory is reconstructive, so related ideas can create false memories sleep related words are processed more deeply than other words are participants were simply guessing with low confidence the list was too long for short term memory capacity

dogs that first received shocks they could not escape later failed to jump a low barrier to escape shocks, even though escape was easy. dogs that had received the same shocks but could stop them by pressing a panel learned to escape quickly. which conclusion is best supported? learning that outcomes are uncontrollable can suppress later coping inescapable shock damaged the dogs' ability to move any exposure to shock at all makes later escape learning much slower the dogs had habituated to shock and no longer felt it

after a concussion, a football player cannot remember the 30 minutes before the hit, but his memories from the previous week and from childhood are intact. what does this pattern suggest? his most recent memories had not yet been fully consolidated he has anterograde amnesia caused by the surgical removal of his hippocampus his older memories are held in sensory memory his older memories are held in short term memory

patient h.m. had much of the medial temporal lobe on both sides removed to treat seizures, including the front portions of both hippocampi and the amygdalae. over several days he practiced tracing a star while seeing it only in a mirror. his accuracy improved steadily, yet each day he said he had never done the task before. which conclusion is best supported? procedural learning does not depend on the hippocampus his hippocampus was required for learning the motor skill his surgery mainly caused retrograde amnesia for childhood he was faking his memory loss to avoid further testing

rats drank sweet water while each lick also triggered a flash of light and a click. then one group was made ill by x ray exposure, and another received foot shocks. later, the ill rats avoided the sweet taste but not the light and click, while the shocked rats avoided the light and click but not the taste. what does this show? animals are biologically prepared to link certain cues to certain outcomes any stimulus can be paired equally well with any consequence, whatever its type taste aversions need many separate pairings before they appear rats cannot detect lights and sounds while they are drinking

participants hear lists and repeat them back in order. average span (items recalled correctly) is shown. list type average span single digits 7 one syllable words 6 five syllable words 3 which conclusion fits best? span depends partly on how long items take to say span is fixed at exactly 7 items for any material longer words are stored in long term memory instead five syllable words are less familiar, so span is 0

rats press a lever for either food pellets or tokens they can trade for food, water or a running wheel. after the rats eat their fill, pressing for pellets drops sharply, but pressing for tokens drops much less. what best explains this? tokens are generalized reinforcers, less hurt by satiation food is a secondary reinforcer, so it loses value after meals tokens are primary reinforcers that satisfy a biological need the rats forgot the link between pellets and lever pressing

while solving problems, participants rate every 15 seconds how close they feel to the answer. for algebra problems, ratings rise steadily before a solution. for riddle like problems, ratings stay low and then jump just before the answer. what does this suggest about the riddle like problems? they are solved by insight, with no sense of gradual progress they are solved by trial and error, with steady gradual progress they are solved by following an algorithm one step at a time they are solved by recalling the answer from a past experience

decades after high school, adults could pick out about 90% of their classmates' photos from a set of strangers' photos, but could recall only a small fraction of classmates' names on their own. what best explains the gap? recognition gives retrieval cues that free recall lacks recall uses long term memory, but recognition does not the photos were stored, but the names were never encoded recognition tests are always easier because of guessing

in a conditioning study, a tone is played just after food is given rather than before it. after many such pairings, dogs salivate very little to the tone. why? the tone never predicted the food, so it signaled nothing backward pairings produce stronger conditioning than forward the food became a conditioned stimulus for the tone dogs cannot learn associations between sounds and food

on a psychiatric unit, patients earn plastic tokens for making their beds and attending group sessions, then trade the tokens for snacks or extra tv time. the tokens act as: secondary (conditioned) reinforcers primary (unlearned, biological) reinforcers negative reinforcers unconditioned stimuli

to learn the term 'osteoclast,' one student repeats it 20 times. another notes that ' clast' means 'break' and pictures cells chewing through bone. why will the second student probably remember the term better? elaborative rehearsal links new items to meaning repetition keeps items in sensory memory longer repeating a word 20 times overloads working memory visual images are stored only as procedural memory

a pharmacist knows a drug's name starts with 'm' and has three syllables, but she can't come up with it until it pops into her head an hour later. this experience shows: a retrieval failure, not loss of the memory decay of the memory trace over time a failure to encode the name in the first place anterograde amnesia for recently learned names

a student keeps checking her email for a reply from an admissions office. replies arrive at unpredictable times, and checking is rewarded only once a reply has come in. which reinforcement schedule is this? variable interval variable ratio fixed interval continuous reinforcement

a patient vividly remembers her doctor warning her about a drug's side effect, but she actually read the warning in a pamphlet in the waiting room. this error is best described as: a source monitoring error retroactive interference anterograde amnesia a flashbulb memory error

in a hypothetical memory study modeled on ebbinghaus's method, a participant needs the numbers of trials shown to recite a list perfectly. a week later she can't recall any of the list. what is her savings score? 60% 40% 8% 250%

patients with severe anterograde amnesia study a list that includes the word motel. later they can't recall the list, but when asked to complete 'mot___' with the first word that comes to mind, they often write motel. this shows that: priming, a form of implicit memory, is intact their explicit memory for the list is intact they are faking their memory loss on purpose procedural memory has replaced semantic memory

to memorize the 12 cranial nerves, a student imagines walking through her house and placing one nerve in each room. during the exam, she mentally walks the same route. which strategy is she using? the method of loci the peg word method chunking maintenance rehearsal

participants who judged whether each trait word (like 'kind') described themselves later remembered more words than participants who judged whether each word described someone else or who judged its meaning. this is the: self reference effect serial position effect misinformation effect spacing effect

a man with years of heavy alcohol use and poor nutrition can't form new memories and confidently fills in memory gaps with made up stories. deficiency of which vitamin is the main cause of this syndrome? thiamine (vitamin b1) vitamin c vitamin d cobalamin (vitamin b12)

during a depressive episode, a patient mostly recalls failures and sad events from her past; when her mood improves, she recalls more happy events. this illustrates: mood congruent memory retrograde amnesia proactive interference the serial position effect

a first year medical student watches a skilled surgeon tie a complex suture on video many times. he pays close attention, remembers each step and wants to succeed, but still can't tie the knot himself. which of bandura's conditions for observational learning is missing? reproduction: the skill to do it attention to the model retention of what was observed motivation to perform it

the graph shows hypothetical lever pressing rates during extinction (no more rewards) for two groups of rats. during training, one group was rewarded for every press, and the other for an unpredictable one third of presses. which line most likely shows the partially reinforced group? line 2, which declines slowly line 1, which declines quickly neither; both groups would extinguish equally fast line 1, since more rewards build more persistence

the table shows a design like leon kamin's blocking experiments in rats. both groups received identical phase 2 training, yet group 1 learned little fear of the tone. why? the light already predicted shock, so the tone added no information in group 1 the tone came too late after the shock to be learned group 1 had already extinguished its fear of the light before phase 2 rats cannot learn about two stimuli at the same time

participants verify 'a canary can sing' faster than 'a canary has skin.' according to collins and quillian's hierarchical network model of semantic memory, why? 'has skin' is stored at a more distant level (animal) 'has skin' is actually a false statement about canaries shorter sentences are always verified faster singing is stored in procedural memory instead

the day after the september 11, 2001 attacks, students wrote down how they heard the news and also an everyday event from the same time. over the following months, both memories became less consistent at about the same rate, but students stayed far more confident in their 9/11 memories. what is the best conclusion? emotional memories feel vivid but are not necessarily more accurate flashbulb memories are recorded permanently and exactly everyday memories decay while emotional memories never change confidence is a reliable sign that a memory is accurate

in 1924, jenkins and dallenbach tested recall of nonsense syllables after intervals spent either asleep or awake. the graph shows an illustrative version of the pattern they reported. which theory of forgetting does this pattern most directly support? interference from waking activity causes much forgetting memories decay at a fixed rate with the passage of time sleep blocks the encoding of new information forgetting happens only within the first hour

keller and marian breland trained a raccoon to drop coins into a box for food. over time, the raccoon instead began rubbing the coins together and dipping them in and out of the box, even though this delayed its food. what does this show? instinctive behaviors can intrude on operantly trained ones operant conditioning can train any behavior equally well the raccoon had learned the task through insight food stopped working as a reinforcer for the raccoon

rats learn to find a platform hidden just under the water in a pool by using cues around the room. the graph shows hypothetical escape times for control rats and rats given a drug that blocks nmda glutamate receptors in the hippocampus. in a separate test, drug treated rats found a clearly visible platform as fast as controls. what is the best conclusion? nmda blockade impairs spatial learning, not swimming or sight the drug impairs vision, so the rats can't see room cues the drug weakens the rats, so they swim more slowly nmda receptors are needed for every kind of movement

the table shows hypothetical results from a dual task study of working memory. participants hold a list of spoken digits in mind while doing a second task. which conclusion best fits baddeley's working memory model? verbal and spatial tasks use partly separate storage systems all tasks draw on a single short term store of 7 items spatial tapping harms verbal memory more than speaking repeating a word improves memory by adding rehearsal

many patients receiving chemotherapy, which causes nausea, begin to feel nauseated as soon as they enter the clinic's waiting room. in this example, nausea triggered by the waiting room is the: unconditioned stimulus unconditioned response conditioned stimulus conditioned response

rats were reinforced with food for lever pressing in sessions 1 5. food was withheld from session 6 onward. session 11 followed a 24 hour rest (figure). which statement best describes session 11? a reliable rise above session 10, consistent with spontaneous recovery a rise within measurement error, so no change from session 10 can be concluded a return to the acquisition rate, consistent with full relearning an extinction burst, because responding increased right after food was withheld

a patient receiving chemotherapy begins to feel nauseated as soon as she walks into the infusion clinic, before any drug is given. in classical conditioning terms, the clinic is the: unconditioned response unconditioned stimulus conditioned stimulus conditioned response

a child used to get candy by whining at the store checkout. his parents decide never to give in again. on the next few trips, his whining becomes louder and longer before it eventually fades. what explains the temporary increase? an extinction burst spontaneous recovery positive reinforcement stimulus generalization

a patient with chronic headaches learns that a pain reliever makes the throbbing stop, and she now reaches for the medicine sooner each time a headache begins. which process best explains the increase in this behavior? positive punishment positive reinforcement negative punishment negative reinforcement

a slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win every 20 pulls. this reinforcement schedule is most likely to produce: a high, steady response rate that is very resistant to extinction a pause after each reward followed by a burst of responding responding that speeds up only as a fixed time interval ends rapid extinction once rewards stop

which of the following are examples of negative punishment? i. a teen loses phone privileges for a week after missing curfew. ii. a driver buckles his seatbelt to stop the car’s beeping. iii. a driver pays a $100 fine for speeding and later drives more slowly. i only ii only ii and iii only i and iii only

children watch a video in which an adult hits an inflatable doll and is then praised. later, left alone with the doll, many of the children hit it the same way. this result best illustrates: habituation classical conditioning observational learning insight learning

participants see 40 words. half are asked of each word, “is it in capital letters?” and half are asked, “does it fit the sentence ‘she ate the ___’?” a surprise recall test follows. in this study, the dependent variable is: the list of 40 words shown to participants the type of question asked about each word the number of words recalled on the surprise test whether the recall test was a surprise

participants heard 10 word lists and recalled them either immediately or after 30 seconds of counting backward (figure). which conclusion is best supported? neither condition showed a recency effect, so short term memory played no role. the delay removed the primacy effect, showing that the first words in each list are held only in short term memory. the delay lowered recall by the same amount at every position, showing general forgetting. the delay removed the recency effect but left primacy intact, consistent with recency depending on short term memory.

a nursing student studied spanish in high school and began italian in college. now, when she tries to recall spanish words, italian words come to mind instead. this is an example of: decay proactive interference retroactive interference source amnesia

a patient with severe anterograde amnesia practices tracing a star while viewing it in a mirror. over three days his speed and accuracy improve steadily, yet each day he insists he has never done the task. this best shows that: procedural (implicit) memory can form without explicit memory of the sessions the patient’s hippocampus is functioning normally episodic memory is required for every kind of learning his improvement reflects sensory adaptation to the mirror rather than any learning

rats injected with an nmda receptor blocker before training fail to learn the location of a hidden platform, but rats given the blocker after they have already learned the location find it normally. which interpretation is best supported? the blocker impairs swimming ability rather than memory. nmda receptors are needed to retrieve memories but not to form them. nmda receptor activity is needed to form new memories, as in long term potentiation, but not to retrieve old ones. nmda receptors are inhibitory gaba receptors that normally prevent learning, so blocking them should help it.

participants watch a video of a car crash and are randomly assigned to answer either “how fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?” or “...when they hit each other?” the “smashed” group gives higher speed estimates. why is random assignment important here? it ensures that the results apply to all eyewitnesses in real courtrooms. it makes it likely that differences in estimates come from the verb rather than from differences between groups. it ensures that participants do not know the hypothesis. it makes each participant's speed estimate more reliable from one test to the next, so scores are more consistent.

a professor finds that students who chose to spread their studying over several days scored 12 points higher on an exam than students who chose to cram the night before. which is the most serious threat to concluding that spacing caused the higher scores? the same professor graded the exams for both groups, so grading standards may have drifted. students who choose to space their studying may differ in motivation or organization from those who cram. both groups took the same exam at the same time. a 12 point difference may be too large to be real.

divers learned word lists either on a beach or underwater and were then tested in the same setting or the other one (figure). which conclusion is best supported? being underwater impaired recall no matter where words were learned. learning on land produced better recall in both test settings. recall was best when the learning and testing environments matched. the test setting had no effect on recall.

a student who moves into a dorm beside a train track is startled by the first few passing trains, but after two weeks she barely reacts, even though the trains are just as loud. which form of learning does this describe? extinction sensitization habituation operant conditioning

in the graph, words at the end of the list are recalled well immediately but poorly after a 30 second distraction. what does this best show? the recency effect depends on short term memory the primacy effect depends on short term memory distraction erases long term memory words in the middle are encoded best

why are the first few words recalled better than the middle words, even after the delay? they were rehearsed more they are still in short term memory they are shorter words they were presented more loudly
in the graph, the response to the tone returns briefly after a 24 hour rest (block 12). this is called spontaneous recovery extinction acquisition stimulus generalization
which schedule in the graph produces the highest, steadiest response rate? variable ratio fixed ratio fixed interval all three are equal

the scalloped pattern of the fixed interval line shows that the animal responds faster as the reward time nears responds at a constant rate stops responding after the first reward is reinforced after a set number of responses

which statement best describes the results in figure 1? the better method depended on the delay before the final test rereading produced better recall than quizzing at both delays tested quizzing produced better recall at both delays tested recall declined by the same amount in both conditions

suppose the reread condition had also been tested 1 day after studying. if its forgetting followed ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, recall at 1 day would most likely be: well below 58%, because most of the loss over the week would occur early about 74%, because the week's loss would be spread evenly across the 7 days about 80%, because memories would hold steady for several days and then fade below 36%, because forgetting is fastest shortly after learning

why did the researchers have each student take only one final test instead of testing everyone at both 5 minutes and 1 week? an early test would itself act as retrieval practice for reread students testing twice would make the study take far too long for the student volunteers one test per student ensured that predicted recall was the same a single test removed the need for random assignment to delays

which statement about the students' predictions is best supported by table 1? reread students greatly overestimated their recall; quiz students were nearly accurate quiz students greatly overestimated their recall; reread students were accurate both groups underestimated how much they would recall after one week both groups predicted their week later recall within two percentage points

the researchers conclude that misleading details are often blended into memory for the video, rather than knowingly repeated from the summary. suppose the test had also asked participants where they had encountered each detail they chose. which result would best support this conclusion? most who chose a misleading detail said they had seen it in the video most who chose a misleading detail said they had read it in the summary most who chose a misleading detail said that they were only guessing most who chose a detail from the video said they had seen it in the video

which statement best describes the results in figure 1? the warning reduced misleading detail answers by the same amount in both summary conditions, neutral and misleading. the warning eliminated the effect of the misleading summary. the warning had a much larger effect after the misleading summary than after the neutral summary. the type of summary had no effect once participants were warned.

which change to the procedure would introduce a confound into the comparison between summary conditions? using a different video of a crime for both summary groups testing all participants after 1 week instead of 48 hours having the misleading summary also be twice as long as the neutral summary adding four more non critical questions to the test for all participants

which conclusions are supported by the data? i. the warning eliminated the misinformation effect. ii. the warning reduced the misinformation effect. iii. some participants chose misleading details even after being warned that the summary contained errors. i only ii only i and iii only ii and iii only

what do the data in table 1 most strongly suggest about eyewitness testimony? a witness's confidence is a poor guide to whether a specific memory is accurate. misleading details are recalled with much lower confidence than true details. confident witnesses are rarely influenced by post event information. confidence ratings measured the same thing as the warning manipulation.
paying for abstinence
in operant terms, the reset of the voucher value after a positive breath sample is best classified as: positive punishment negative reinforcement negative punishment extinction

which comparison at week 24 is best supported by figure 1? escalating vouchers produced clearly higher abstinence than standard care, but not clearly higher than fixed vouchers. escalating vouchers produced clearly higher abstinence than both other conditions, including fixed vouchers, at every time point. fixed vouchers produced clearly higher abstinence than standard care. all three conditions had statistically indistinguishable abstinence.

the researchers attribute the fall in abstinence after week 12 to the withdrawal of the vouchers. which added condition would best test this explanation against the alternative that abstinence simply declines as more time passes since quitting? an escalating voucher group whose vouchers continue through week 24 a standard care group that is followed through week 36 instead of week 24 a fixed voucher group that gives breath samples once per week a voucher group paid for every sample, whether negative or not

which statements about the design of this study are correct? i. random assignment protects against group differences that arise after assignment, such as unequal dropout. ii. because dropouts were counted as smoking, reported abstinence rates are, if anything, underestimates. iii. verifying abstinence with breath co reduces bias that could come from self report. i and ii only i and iii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

the researchers want to apply these findings to smokers who have not sought help to quit. the main limitation is a threat to: internal validity, because the three conditions were not randomly assigned to participants construct validity, because breath co does not measure smoking statistical conclusion validity, because the sample was too large external validity, because participants were treatment seeking clinic patients
schedules of reinforcement and extinction

based on figure 1, which factor had the larger effect on training response rate: whether food depended on number of presses (ratio versus interval) or whether it was predictable (fixed versus variable)? ratio versus interval, changing average rate by about 40 responses per minute predictability, because vr 10 exceeded fr 10 by about 20 responses per minute the two factors had equal effects of about 20 responses per minute each ratio versus interval, but only among fixed schedules, as vr and vi rates were similar
