in a classic problem from tversky and kahneman (data in the table), 85% of a city's cabs are green and 15% are blue. a witness who identifies cab colors correctly 80% of the time says a hit and run cab was blue. most people say the chance the cab really was blue is 80%. what is the actual probability, and why do people get it wrong? about 41%; they neglect the base rate of blue cabs about 80%; the witness's accuracy settles it about 15%; the witness adds no information about 68%; both percentages must be multiplied

johnson and newport tested the english grammar of chinese and korean immigrants who had all lived in the united states for several years, and compared them with native english speakers. the graph shows illustrative values matching the pattern they reported. which conclusion is best supported? grammar learning is easiest during a sensitive period in childhood years of exposure explain the scores, not the age of arrival adult learners eventually reach native like levels of grammar children and adults learn grammar equally well

after a stroke, a patient speaks fluently with normal rhythm, but her sentences contain made up words and make little sense, and she has great difficulty understanding what others say. damage is most likely in the: left inferior frontal lobe (broca's area) left posterior superior temporal lobe (wernicke's area) right occipital lobe arcuate fasciculus only, with both language areas intact

to test whether caffeine speeds reaction time, researchers tested 30 participants after a placebo drink on monday and after a caffeinated drink on tuesday. reaction times were faster on tuesday. what is the most serious flaw in this design? the sample is too small to include both conditions. practice effects are confounded with caffeine because every participant received the conditions in the same order. using the same participants in both conditions increases variability caused by individual differences between people. reaction time is not a valid measure of alertness.

in a problem solving study, participants must attach a candle to a wall using a box of tacks and matches. when the tacks are given inside the box, 40% solve the problem within 10 minutes by tacking the empty box to the wall as a shelf. when the tacks are given beside an empty box, 85% solve it. which interpretation is best supported? participants given the full box solved the problem more often because they had more materials. presenting the box as a container made it harder to see the box’s other use, showing functional fixedness. the difference reflects the availability heuristic, because the tacks were easier to see. both groups solved the problem equally well, so presentation had no effect.

after a week of news coverage of a plane crash, a traveler decides to drive 800 miles instead of flying because she now believes flying is more dangerous, even though driving has a much higher fatality rate per mile. her judgment best illustrates: functional fixedness the representativeness heuristic anchoring the availability heuristic

in a town, 70 of every 100 adults are farmers and 30 are librarians. a randomly chosen resident is described as “quiet, tidy and fond of books.” most people answer “librarian” without considering how many farmers there are. their reasoning best illustrates: anchoring, relying on the first number given the availability heuristic, relying on recent examples the representativeness heuristic, with neglect of the base rate functional fixedness, seeing only one use for the information

a physician who suspects pneumonia notes every test result that fits pneumonia and dismisses a normal chest x ray as a technical error. her reasoning best illustrates: the gambler’s fallacy the framing effect hindsight bias confirmation bias

a sleep technician sees an eeg with bursts of 12 14 hz activity (sleep spindles) and sharp k complexes, with no rapid eye movements. the patient is most likely in which stage? rem sleep n3 (slow wave) sleep n2 (stage 2) sleep relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed

a sleep lab recorded the minutes of n3 and rem sleep in each roughly 90 minute cycle across one night in healthy adults (figure). if a person is woken by an alarm after only 3 cycles instead of 5, the sleep lost will be mostly: n3 sleep, because n3 is concentrated late in the night rem sleep, because rem periods grow longer in later cycles equal amounts of n3 and rem sleep neither n3 nor rem sleep, because both occur only in the first 3 cycles
a pharmacology student is sorting drugs by class. which are cns depressants? i. alcohol ii. benzodiazepines iii. amphetamine i and ii only i only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

a researcher studying cocaine in rats finds that the drug’s rewarding effect disappears when dopamine signaling is blocked in one brain region. this region is most likely the: medulla, which regulates arousal through breathing occipital cortex, which processes the visual reward cues tied to the drug cerebellum, which stores learned drug seeking habits nucleus accumbens, the target of the mesolimbic pathway from the ventral tegmental area

a man who regularly injects heroin in his own bedroom survives a dose that later kills him when he injects the same amount in an unfamiliar motel room. which explanation is best supported by conditioning research? his tolerance disappeared because he had not used the drug for a few hours. cues in his usual setting trigger a conditioned compensatory response that counteracts the drug; those cues were absent in the new room. the new room's cues produced a conditioned response that mimicked the drug, so the two effects added together and became lethal. heroin is metabolized more slowly in unfamiliar environments.

a researcher finds that speakers of a language with separate basic words for light blue and dark blue tell those shades apart faster than english speakers do. she concludes that language shapes perception. what is the most important limitation of this study? language was not manipulated, so other cultural differences between the groups could explain the result. faster discrimination by these speakers would actually show that language has no effect at all on perception. reaction time cannot measure perceptual differences between colors. the study should have tested speakers of only one language.

a 3 year old says, “i goed to the park and seed two mouses.” which conclusion is best supported by this kind of error? children learn language only by imitating adult speech. children extract grammatical rules and apply them, even where adults use exceptions. the child has a language disorder affecting broca’s area. the child has already passed the sensitive period for learning the grammar of a first language.

a patient speaks rapidly with normal rhythm, saying, “the tremble went over the shimmer to get the thing,” and cannot follow simple spoken instructions. damage is most likely in which area? the cerebellum broca's area in the left frontal lobe, near the motor cortex the primary motor cortex wernicke’s area in the left posterior temporal lobe

in a dichotic listening task, participants repeat aloud a story played to the right ear and ignore a story in the left ear. they cannot report the left ear story, but many notice when their own name is spoken in it. this finding is most consistent with: an early filter model, in which unattended input is fully blocked before any meaning is analyzed attenuation theory, in which unattended input is weakened but still processed for meaning attention being divided equally between the two ears inattentional blindness for visual stimuli

a company develops a new reasoning test for college admissions and compares it with an established test (table). which conclusion is best supported? the new test is valid but unreliable. the new test is reliable but shows little predictive validity for gpa. the new test is both more reliable and more valid than the established test. the new test is neither reliable nor valid.

each participant completes a reaction time task once after a normal night of sleep and once after a night without sleep, and every participant does the rested session first. which change would best fix the main design flaw? recruit more participants and keep the same order. randomly vary the order so that half of the participants do the sleep deprived session first. use a different reaction time task in each session. tell participants the hypothesis so that they try equally hard during both of the sessions.

which pattern does the graph show? rem periods grow longer later in the night deep sleep (n3) increases late in the night rem sleep occurs only at the start of the night the sleeper stays in one stage all night

in this study, 40 students were randomly assigned to sleep or stay awake after learning a word list. what is the independent variable? sleep or no sleep the number of words recalled the 20 word list the students' ages

in a lexical decision task, participants decide as quickly as possible whether a string of letters is a word. they respond faster to nurse when it follows doctor than when it follows bread. which explanation best fits this result? spreading activation: doctor activates linked nodes in a semantic network, partly priming nurse retroactive interference: the second word disrupts recall of the first, which frees up attention for nurse the serial position effect: words that appear later in a list are recalled better because they are recent proactive interference: earlier learning makes it harder to process related information presented later

participants verify "a robin is a bird" faster than "a penguin is a bird." how does a spreading activation network model (such as collins and loftus's) account for this result? the link between robin and bird is shorter or stronger, so activation travels between them faster robin is stored fewer levels below bird in a strict hierarchy, so fewer steps are needed to reach it penguin is stored in procedural memory, whereas robin is stored in semantic memory, which is faster penguin activates bird more strongly than robin does, which slows the decision through interference
sleep and memory

a critic argues that the sleep group's advantage reflects stronger initial learning rather than changes to the memories during the 12 hour delay. which feature of the procedure most directly weakens this criticism? the list was repeated until each participant reached the same recall criterion before the delay at test, participants were cued with the first word of each pair rather than asked for free recall scorers who divided the night into sleep stages did not know participants' recall scores participants in both groups were told not to rehearse the word pairs during the delay
which eeg pattern would most likely be prominent during the sleep stage linked to better recall? alpha waves beta waves delta waves sleep spindles only

which is the biggest weakness in this study's design? the groups learned and were tested at different times of day the word pairs may have been too easy for participants in both groups recall was measured as the number of pairs remembered both groups studied the identical list of word pairs

besides missing sleep, what else could explain the wake group's lower recall? proactive interference from information learned before the word pairs retroactive interference from new information encountered during the day sensory adaptation to the word pairs during the waking hours learned helplessness from failing to recall pairs during the day
two tasks, one mind?

in the verbal span task, letters appeared on a screen. in the model, printed items enter the verbal store only after being silently pronounced by the same articulatory process used for rehearsal. normally, similar sounding letters (b, d, g, p) are harder to recall in order than dissimilar letters (f, k, r, x). based on the model, under articulatory suppression this disadvantage for visually presented letters should: shrink, because suppression keeps printed letters from being recoded into the phonological loop grow, because suppression adds more speech sounds that resemble the letters being remembered stay the same, because suppression blocks rehearsal but not how letters are recoded before storage shrink for spoken and printed letters alike, because suppression empties the phonological store itself

the pattern of results in figure 1 is best described as: a main effect of secondary task only, with both secondary tasks impairing both primary tasks equally a main effect of primary task only, with verbal span always higher than spatial span no effect of secondary tasks, since all spans remained above four items an interaction, in which each secondary task impaired mainly the primary task of its own type

why did the researchers counterbalance the order of the six task by condition combinations? to prevent practice and fatigue effects from being confounded with condition to allow the results to generalize to people outside the university who differ in age and education to ensure that each participant was assigned to only one condition to keep participants unaware of the study's hypothesis

which statements are supported by figure 1? i. spatial tapping reduced spatial span more than articulatory suppression did. ii. the data do not show a clear effect of articulatory suppression on spatial span. iii. because the design was within subjects, the results can be generalized to all adults. i only iii only i and ii only i, ii and iii

suppose a third secondary task, generating a random sequence of digits aloud, heavily taxes the attentional control system. based on the model, this task should: impair verbal span only, since digits are verbal impair spatial span only impair both verbal and spatial span impair neither span
switching languages, switching tasks

which conclusion is best supported by figure 1? the bilingual advantage seen in study 1 was much smaller when the groups were matched on family background bilingual students switch tasks faster than monolingual students do, whatever their family background or income monolingual students made more sorting errors on switch trials than either bilingual group matching on family income doubled the switch cost of the bilingual students in study 2

why is switch cost, rather than reaction time on switch trials alone, the better dependent variable for comparing these groups? a group 40 ms faster on every trial would show the same switch cost, so it isolates rule changes switch cost converts the between groups comparison into a true experiment with random assignment because accuracy was above 95%, switch trial reaction time could not be scored for most participants switch cost includes errors as well as response times, so it captures speed and accuracy together

which feature of study 1 most weakens the claim that bilingualism itself caused the smaller switch cost? language group differed from the monolingual group in family background as well as language use the task measured reaction time rather than asking students to rate their own attention and focus participants were university students rather than a random sample of all adults both groups completed the same number of repeat and switch trials

the color shape task mainly measures shifting between rules. which added measure would most directly test the passage's proposal that bilinguals strengthen inhibition of competing responses? a stroop task comparing incongruent with congruent color word trials a test of how many words in each language participants can later recall a version of the color shape task with more switch trials and fewer repeats a version of the color shape task with a longer interval between cue and shape

a researcher wants to test whether bilingual experience causes better executive control. which design would best support a causal conclusion? randomly assigning monolingual children to a second language program or a matched program, testing before and after comparing adults who chose to learn a second language as adults with adults who chose not to, on the same switching task surveying bilingual adults about how often they switch languages each day and correlating it with their switch costs testing a larger sample of bilingual and monolingual university students
anchoring in the clinic

which finding best indicates that physicians' shifts toward the triage note reflect the anchoring heuristic rather than sensible reliance on a nurse's clinical judgment? estimates still shifted toward notes labeled as randomly generated estimates after the high anchor were well above the risk model's value of 35% estimates moved in opposite directions after the low and the high triage notes years of experience were not related to the size of the shift toward the note

under standard instructions, how far apart were the mean estimates after low and high anchors? about 33 percentage points about 60 percentage points about 11 percentage points about 19 percentage points

what does the effect of listing opposing findings suggest about anchoring? considering evidence against an impression reduces its pull. listing findings makes physicians agree more closely with the nurse. listing findings works only when no anchor is present. anchoring cannot be reduced by any change in instructions.

why is the risk model's 35% estimate important to the study? it is a benchmark for judging bias it is the anchor that every physician was shown it shows that the physicians were randomly assigned to the anchor conditions it proves the patient had a heart attack

physicians' belief that the note did not influence them is best explained by: anchoring operating largely outside conscious awareness the physicians having ignored the triage note the triage note having been shown only after the estimates experienced physicians being immune to anchoring
survival or mortality?

a critic argues that the shift in choices reflects participants misreading the percentages, not a framing effect in which equivalent outcomes are valued differently. which finding most directly weakens this critique? participants with high numeracy still showed a framing effect choices of radiation were about 25% when both frames were shown together the order in which the two treatments were described was counterbalanced patients in the study were not facing a lung cancer diagnosis themselves

which conclusion is best supported by figure 1? the mortality frame raised radiation choices in every group. physicians were unaffected by framing because of their medical training and experience. the survival frame raised radiation choices in all three groups. patients were much more affected by framing than physicians.

according to prospect theory, why did the mortality frame favor radiation? a 10% chance of dying in surgery feels like a large loss. a 90% chance of surviving surgery feels like a large loss. people seek risk when outcomes are framed as gains. radiation has a better long term outcome than surgery.

what does the result with both frames suggest? seeing both frames weakens a frame's pull. seeing both frames makes radiation the most popular choice. seeing both frames makes everyone choose surgery. presenting both frames has no effect on choices.

why did each participant see only one frame? seeing both would reveal the manipulation so the researchers could compare patients with physicians so that every participant would choose surgery because the two frames contain different statistics
pouring water into a taller glass

based on the passage's account of piaget's stages, which task would the 9 year olds who conserved in figure 1 most likely still find difficult? reasoning about what follows from a purely hypothetical premise judging that a row of coins keeps its number when spread out searching for a toy after watching it being hidden under a cloth describing what a doll seated across a model would see from its side
according to figure 1, at what age did a majority first conserve when the experimenter poured? 7 5 6 9

which conclusion is best supported by the puppet condition? some children understood conservation but answered to fit a cue. puppets confuse children so they cannot judge amounts correctly. conservation develops much later than piaget proposed. older children were affected by the puppet more than younger ones.

suppose the experimenter had poured the juice from one short glass into a dish that was wider and shallower than the glass, instead of into a tall, thin glass. based on the explanations given by children who did not conserve in the study, these children would most likely say that the dish holds: less juice, because the juice does not come up as high in it more juice, because the dish is much wider than the glass was the same amount, because the juice could be poured back again the same amount, because the dish is lower but also wider

which feature of the design limits conclusions about development within individual children? different children were tested at each age each of the six age groups contained 25 children both versions used the same glasses the children explained their answers
tired residents, missed signals

according to the passage's two process model, if eeg were recorded on the first 10 hour recovery night, how would the 4 hour group's sleep most likely differ from their sleep before the study? more slow wave sleep, concentrated early in the night less slow wave sleep, because the brain had adapted to short sleep more stage 1 sleep, because the circadian process had been disrupted no change in sleep stages, since recovery did not restore performance

according to figure 1, how did lapses in the 4 hour group change over 14 days? they rose steadily to about nine times baseline. they rose for 2 days and then returned to baseline. they stayed the same as in the 8 hour group. they fell as participants adapted to short sleep.

what does the pattern of sleepiness ratings in the 6 hour group suggest? people may feel adapted while still getting worse. people accurately sense how impaired they become over time. six hours of sleep is enough to avoid impairment. sleepiness and lapses always change together.

which conclusion follows from the recovery results? recovering from sleep debt can take over two nights. two nights of long sleep fully reverse any sleep debt. short sleep causes permanent loss of attention. recovery is faster after 4 hours than after 6 hours.

a critic argues that the 4 hour group's rising lapses reflect boredom from repeating the same vigilance task every 2 days, not sleep loss. which aspect of the study most directly weakens this argument? the 8 hour group did the same task on the same schedule, with flat lapses. the task was given at the same times of day on every test day for all groups. sleepiness ratings in the 6 hour group leveled off after the first few days. two nights of 10 hours in bed did not fully restore the 4 hour group's performance.
accents and the age of arrival

critics argue that the age of arrival effect on accent reflects differences in english exposure rather than a sensitive period. which comparison would best separate these explanations? early and late arrivals matched on daily english use and years of residence speakers from korea compared with speakers from china who arrived at the same age accent ratings compared with grammar scores within the same participants accent ratings from trained linguists compared with ratings from ordinary listeners
according to figure 1, which skill declined more steeply with later arrival? accent grammar neither skill declined both declined equally

which finding is hardest to explain with a strict biological cutoff for accent? some adult arrivals were rated native like. accent scores fell with later age of arrival. grammar scores fell with later age of arrival. raters didn't know speakers' backgrounds.

the correlation between daily english use and accent among late arrivals suggests that: practice still matters after the sensitive period years of residence explain accent better than daily use daily english use is caused by having a native like accent late arrivals cannot improve their accent at all

suppose the raters had known each speaker's age of arrival. which result would be least open to the resulting bias? the decline in grammar test scores with later arrival the decline in accent ratings with later arrival the native like accent ratings given to some adult arrivals the correlation of accent with daily english use among late arrivals
sleeping on a problem

which pattern of response times for one participant across retest trials would best indicate insight rather than gradual improvement from practice? a flat stretch followed by an abrupt, lasting drop a steady decline that slowly leveled off over many trials a slow decline followed by a return to the starting speed fast responses that stayed the same from the very first trial
according to figure 1, about how many times as many night sleep participants as day wake participants discovered the rule? about 2.6 about 59 about 1.2 about 36

why was a night wake group included in addition to a day wake group? to separate the effect of sleep from time of day to show that sleepiness improves problem solving to give every group the same amount of practice to test whether the rule could be found without practice

what does the second experiment show? sleep helped only when there was something to restructure. sleep helped discovery even without any initial practice. practice alone was enough for most people to find the rule. staying awake helped more than sleep without practice.

which conclusion is best supported by the slow wave sleep finding? deep sleep may help restructure new information. rem sleep alone caused participants to find the rule. more slow wave sleep proves that sleep causes insight. slow wave sleep makes participants sleepier at retest.

name: Motivation, emotion & stress
t: a man's heart races during an exam. he decides he is excited rather than anxious, and then he feels excited. which theory of emotion best fits? james lange (bodily feedback) cannon bard (simultaneous) schachter singer (two factor) yerkes dodson (arousal law)
according to the yerkes dodson law, performance on a moderately difficult task is best when arousal is: very low moderate very high unrelated to arousal
a runner trains for a marathon to win a medal and recognition. which theory of motivation best explains this? drive reduction theory incentive theory instinct theory arousal theory

a researcher wants to measure students' intrinsic motivation for solving puzzles without relying on what they say. which measure is best? time spent on puzzles in an unobserved free period with other options number of puzzles solved while the experimenter watches and offers a prize students' answers to a question asking how much they enjoy puzzles number of puzzles solved during a timed test that counts toward a grade

a hospital wants nurses to keep doing quality improvement projects for their own sake, long after any program ends. according to self determination theory, which approach is most likely to work? let nurses choose projects and give feedback on their progress pay a cash bonus to each nurse for every project completed assign the projects and monitor each nurse closely every week publicly rank nurses by the number of projects each one finished

a survey of people in over 120 countries found that meeting social and respect needs was linked to positive feelings even among people whose food and shelter needs were not fully met. which conclusion does this most directly support? higher needs can matter before lower needs are fully satisfied basic needs must be completely met before any other need matters social needs matter only in wealthy countries with secure food supplies the survey shows that meeting social needs causes people to feel happier

american and japanese students watched a gruesome film. when alone, both groups showed similar facial expressions of disgust and fear. when an experimenter sat in the room, the japanese students more often masked these expressions with polite smiles. what does this show? basic expressions are shared, but cultural rules shape when they are shown facial expressions of emotion are learned separately in each culture the japanese students felt less disgust than the american students did the experimenter's presence made both groups show more negative expressions

a student narrowly avoids a car crash. his heart pounds within seconds, and an hour later his blood glucose is still high. which pairing best explains the fast and the slower responses? fast: sympathetic nerves trigger epinephrine; slower: hpa axis cortisol fast: hpa axis cortisol; slower: sympathetic nerves trigger epinephrine fast: parasympathetic nerves; slower: sympathetic nerves and the adrenals fast: cortisol from the adrenal medulla; slower: epinephrine from the cortex
arousal theory says people are motivated to: keep an optimal level of arousal keep arousal as low as possible at all times always seek the highest arousal available avoid all stimulation

drive reduction theory proposes that behavior is motivated by: a desire to reduce internal tension from unmet biological needs a desire to maintain an optimal, moderate level of arousal innate, fixed behavior patterns shaped by evolution the pull of external incentives such as money, grades or praise

according to the james lange theory, emotion occurs when: we perceive our body's physical reaction to a stimulus body reaction and emotion happen at the same time, independently we label arousal with a cognitive explanation the amygdala releases an emotion directly

the cannon bard theory says that: arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently emotional experience follows from the perception of bodily arousal emotion results from arousal plus a cognitive label for it emotion begins with a cognitive appraisal before any arousal
in selye's general adaptation syndrome, which stage comes after alarm? resistance exhaustion recovery denial
which hormone is the main long term stress hormone released by the adrenal cortex? cortisol insulin oxytocin melatonin

in lazarus's appraisal model, secondary appraisal is: judging whether you have the resources to cope with a stressor judging whether a situation is threatening, challenging or harmless reassessing a stressor after an initial coping attempt the body's alarm reaction during the first stage of stress

a student who used to read for fun starts getting paid per book and later stops reading when the payments end. this is the: overjustification effect drive reduction effect yerkes dodson effect incentive salience
a runner chooses between two equally appealing races scheduled on the same day. this is which type of conflict? approach approach avoidance avoidance approach avoidance double approach avoidance
smiling when you are not happy can slightly improve your mood. this supports the: facial feedback hypothesis cannon bard theory opponent process theory drive reduction theory
which coping strategy focuses on changing the stressful situation itself? problem focused coping emotion focused coping denial avoidance

chronic stress can make people more likely to get sick. which explanation best fits? long term cortisol release suppresses immune function stress increases white blood cell counts permanently stress lowers heart rate stress raises melatonin all day

self determination theory says people need three things for healthy motivation. which set is correct? autonomy, competence and relatedness food, water, shelter and safety money, status and power arousal, drive, incentive and reward
which brain structure, besides the amygdala, is especially important in regulating emotion through planning and reasoning? prefrontal cortex occipital lobe cerebellum medulla

workers who face high job demands but have little control over their work show more stress related illness than workers with high demands and high control. what does this suggest? perceived control reduces the impact of stress high job demands alone cause all of the stress control increases stress type of job has no effect on a worker's health

a patient's heart races after drinking too much coffee. they attend a party and feel very excited and happy. according to the two factor theory, why? they labeled their caffeine arousal as excitement because of the setting caffeine directly produced happiness without any cognitive labeling the party caused excitement first, which then raised their heart rate their arousal and happiness arose at the same time but independently

research on hunger finds that damage to the lateral hypothalamus in animals leads to a loss of interest in food, while damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus leads to overeating. what does this suggest? the hypothalamus contains areas that both start and stop eating hunger signals come mainly from the stomach, not the brain the lateral hypothalamus signals fullness and stops eating the hypothalamus controls thirst, while hunger is set elsewhere

using the curve shown, consider two students before the same exam: one is so relaxed she is nearly asleep, and the other is so anxious that his hands shake. both perform poorly. which advice best fits the curve? raise arousal for the sleepy student; lower it for the anxious one lower arousal for both students, since less arousal always helps raise arousal for both students, since more arousal always helps lower arousal for the sleepy student; raise it for the anxious one
according to the hierarchy shown, a person who has just lost their home and has no food would focus mainly on which level? physiological needs esteem needs self actualization love and belonging

a goose sees an egg outside its nest and rolls it back with the underside of its bill. if a researcher removes the egg partway, the goose completes the rolling motion anyway. which view of motivation does this best support? instinct theory: inborn action patterns run to completion incentive theory: the egg is a reward that pulls behavior drive reduction theory: the goose acts to reduce hunger arousal theory: the goose seeks an optimal level of stimulation

adults reported their major life events, their daily hassles and their health symptoms over a year (hypothetical correlations). measure correlation with symptoms major life events r = 0.15 daily hassles r = 0.40 which conclusion is justified? daily hassles were more strongly associated with symptoms than major events daily hassles cause illness, while major life events have no effect on health major life events were more strongly associated with symptoms than hassles neither stressor is related to symptoms, since both correlations are below 0.5

a researcher studying fear records a participant's skin conductance, codes her facial expressions from video, and asks her to rate how afraid she feels. which emotion components do these three measures target, in order? physiological, behavioral, cognitive behavioral, physiological, cognitive cognitive, behavioral, physiological physiological, cognitive, behavioral

when a person faces a stressor, which sequence correctly describes the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (hpa) axis? hypothalamus releases crh → anterior pituitary releases acth → adrenal cortex releases cortisol hypothalamus releases acth → posterior pituitary releases crh → adrenal medulla releases cortisol adrenal cortex releases crh → hypothalamus releases acth → anterior pituitary releases cortisol anterior pituitary releases crh → hypothalamus releases acth → adrenal medulla releases epinephrine

a woman diets and loses 10 kg, but her metabolism slows and her hunger rises until she regains most of the weight. which idea best explains this? set point theory of body weight incentive theory of motivation the facial feedback hypothesis opponent process theory of emotion

according to masters and johnson, what is the correct order of the human sexual response cycle? excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution plateau, excitement, orgasm, resolution excitement, orgasm, plateau, resolution arousal, orgasm, refractory, plateau

a student learns that an exam is next week. she first asks herself, 'is this a threat, a challenge, or no big deal?' in lazarus's model, this step is called: primary appraisal secondary appraisal reappraisal problem focused coping

a man has cared for his parent with dementia for two years with no breaks. he is exhausted, catches every cold that goes around and feels unable to cope. in selye's general adaptation syndrome, he is most likely in which stage? exhaustion alarm resistance recovery

eeg studies of emotion (for example, by richard davidson) found that greater resting activity in the left prefrontal cortex is most associated with: positive, approach related emotions negative, withdrawal related emotions a complete lack of emotional response higher risk of panic attacks

a medical student is offered a prestigious residency that she really wants, but it would mean moving far away from her family. which type of motivational conflict is she facing? approach avoidance approach approach avoidance avoidance multiple approach approach

a hiker sees a snake on the trail, thinks 'that could be venomous,' and only then feels fear as her heart starts pounding. which theory of emotion fits this order best? lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory the james lange theory the schachter singer two factor theory the facial feedback hypothesis

a retired surgeon has a stable income, a loving family and the respect of her colleagues. she now spends her time learning to paint, wanting to reach her full creative potential. according to maslow, which need is she pursuing? self actualization esteem love and belonging safety

on her first skydive, a woman feels terror during the jump and mild relief afterward. after 100 jumps, she feels little fear during the jump but intense exhilaration afterward. which theory explains this shift? opponent process theory drive reduction theory two factor theory self determination theory

in one year, a man gets married, moves to a new city and starts a job he wanted. he is happy about all three, yet his score on the holmes and rahe social readjustment rating scale is high. why? the scale counts any change that needs adjustment, good or bad the scale counts only negative events, so it must be scored wrong the scale measures personality traits, not life events at all positive events count only when they cause a physical illness

a patient with an incurable illness cannot change her diagnosis, so she practices meditation, journals and focuses on the meaning she finds in her family. this is an example of: emotion focused coping problem focused coping displacement approach avoidance conflict

after a frightening car accident, a mother calls her sister and gathers her children close rather than fighting or fleeing. shelley taylor proposed this pattern, linked to oxytocin release, as a stress response called: tend and befriend learned helplessness rest and digest reaction formation

walter cannon criticized the james lange theory of emotion. which point formed part of his critique? bodily arousal patterns are too similar across emotions to tell them apart emotions occur only after a person consciously labels a stimulus facial expressions of emotion differ completely from culture to culture emotions are learned through reinforcement rather than felt in the body

early research on 'type a' behavior linked it to heart disease. later studies found which component to be the most toxic predictor of coronary heart disease? hostility and anger time urgency and impatience high achievement drive working long hours

according to the yerkes dodson law, how does the optimal level of arousal for a complex surgical procedure compare with that for a simple, well practiced task like taking a pulse? it is lower for the complex task it is higher for the complex task it is the same for both tasks it is zero for the complex task

people with high need for achievement (studied by david mcclelland and john atkinson) are given a choice of tasks. which will they usually choose? moderately difficult tasks with a realistic chance of success very easy tasks where success is almost guaranteed and failure is unlikely nearly impossible tasks where failure has an excuse tasks chosen at random with no regard to difficulty

people with fully satisfied biological needs still ride roller coasters, explore new places and solve puzzles for fun. which theory is most challenged by this observation? drive reduction theory arousal theory incentive theory self determination theory

according to figure 1, the nursing station was most similar to: a midpoint between patient rooms and break room the break room in every behavior that was measured the patient rooms in every behavior that was measured neither setting, with the highest rate of formal language

why did humor and complaints drop when an administrator entered the break room? the administrator turned the back stage into a front stage. the administrator banned humor in the break room that day. nurses had finished their breaks when the administrator came in. administrators are part of nurses' primary group.

who helps you find a job?

a reader concludes from table 1 that an acquaintance is a more effective source of job leads than a close friend, because weak ties produced twice as many jobs as strong ties. which consideration most undermines this inference? most people have far more acquaintances than close ties, so a larger share need not mean more leads per tie. weak ties were defined by how often workers saw the contact rather than by how warmly they felt about the person. formal channels and direct application together accounted for nearly half of the jobs that workers found. workers who found jobs through weak ties gained more in wages than workers who found jobs through strong ties.

a phlebotomist in the study heard about her job from a former coworker to whom she feels very close but whom she sees only about three times a year. how did the researchers classify this contact, and why? as a weak tie, because contact was less than once a month as a strong tie, because she feels very close to this person as a strong tie, because the contact had worked in the same field as a formal channel, because the contact was a former coworker
which factor could confound the link between weak ties and higher wages? education level which county the workers lived in the workers' job titles the number of interviews conducted
recent movers relied more on formal channels. this best illustrates that social capital takes time formal channels give better jobs movers have more strong ties networks don't affect job searches

which change would best test whether weak ties cause better job outcomes? follow workers over time, adjusting for education interview only workers who used strong ties ask workers to rate their own job satisfaction study a different occupation

name: Social thinking
t: a doctor assumes a patient missed an appointment because he is irresponsible, without considering that his bus broke down. this is: self serving bias in judging others fundamental attribution error actor observer bias halo effect

a hiring manager believes older adults learn new software slowly, feels uneasy around older applicants and rejects most of their applications. the company then requires age blind resume screening. his rejections of older applicants drop, but a survey shows he still feels uneasy around them. what changed? discrimination dropped while his prejudice remained his prejudice disappeared while discrimination continued his stereotype was corrected, which ended the discrimination his prejudice dropped, and that caused fewer rejections

a famous athlete praises a sports drink in a tv ad she was paid $2 million to make. viewers are less convinced that she really likes the drink than when she praises it in an unpaid interview. which attribution principle explains this? discounting her liking when payment could explain it making the fundamental attribution error about the athlete using high consensus to attribute her praise to the drink showing a self serving bias in judging the athlete's motives

participants watched a woman appear to receive painful shocks in a learning task. when told they could later reward her with money, they rated her favorably. when told nothing could be done for her, they rated her as less likable and less worthy. what best explains the second group's reaction? a just world belief, which leads people to blame victims they can't help the actor observer bias, which blames situations for one's own failures cognitive dissonance about having agreed to give the shocks themselves the halo effect, which spreads one positive trait to an overall impression

a clinician dismisses a patient's use of cupping, a traditional practice from her culture, as 'primitive superstition' and refuses to discuss it, though it poses no risk with her treatment. which concept best describes the clinician's view? ethnocentrism cultural relativism xenocentrism culture shock

the actor observer bias means people tend to: explain their own behavior by situation, but others' by personality explain their own behavior by personality, but others' by situation credit successes to themselves and failures to the situation overestimate personality causes for everyone's behavior equally

the halo effect occurs when: one positive trait leads to positive judgments about other traits one negative trait outweighs many positive traits in judgments first impressions anchor all later judgments of a person people see their own group as more varied than other groups

a self fulfilling prophecy occurs when: expectations lead to behavior that makes those expectations come true people notice only evidence that confirms their expectations people believe they had predicted an outcome after learning what happened fear of confirming a stereotype lowers a person's performance

stereotype threat is: underperforming from worry about confirming a stereotype of one's group treating members of a group unfairly because of a stereotype held about them rising to meet others' high expectations about one's abilities holding negative attitudes toward members of another group

according to the contact hypothesis, prejudice is reduced when groups: interact as equals working toward shared goals compete with each other for limited resources are kept apart to reduce chances for conflict learn facts about each other without direct contact

institutional discrimination is: unfair treatment built into the policies of organizations or society unfair treatment by one prejudiced individual toward another person negative attitudes that members of one group hold about another oversimplified, generalized beliefs about the traits of a social group
prejudice toward people in other groups, combined with favoring your own, is linked to: in group bias the mere exposure effect the halo effect altruism

a professor assumes a student who failed an exam is lazy, ignoring that the student was ill. this is: the fundamental attribution error the self serving bias the just world hypothesis about others the halo effect in grading
someone says 'i won the game because i'm talented, but lost because the referee was unfair.' this is: self serving bias fundamental attribution error actor observer bias hindsight bias

kelley's covariation model uses consistency, distinctiveness and consensus to decide whether a behavior is caused by the person or the situation. if everyone reacts the same way (high consensus) and the person reacts this way only in this situation (high distinctiveness), the cause is most likely: the situation the person's personality random chance biology

a hiring manager unknowingly rates resumes with typically male names more favorably than identical resumes with typically female names. this shows: implicit (unconscious) bias explicit (conscious) prejudice self serving bias stereotype threat in the applicants

people in individualist cultures (like the united states) make the fundamental attribution error more often than people in collectivist cultures. why? collectivist cultures stress social context, so people weigh situations more collectivist cultures value modesty, so people blame themselves more genetic differences between the two groups produce their different attribution styles people in individualist cultures have less contact with other people

the implicit association test measures: how quickly people pair concepts, to detect automatic associations how strongly people endorse openly prejudiced statements on a written survey physiological arousal when people view members of other groups how accurately people recall the faces of other groups

a clinic finds that patients from a minority group are less likely to be offered pain medication, even when reported pain levels are the same. which concept best explains this pattern? bias (often implicit) leading to discrimination in care stereotype threat lowering patients' reports of pain the self serving bias among the treating clinicians patients' own preferences to avoid pain medication
a medical student notices that after hearing a patient's diagnosis, she 'knew it all along.' this is: hindsight bias confirmation bias anchoring the halo effect

a doctor sticks with an initial diagnosis even after new test results point elsewhere. which biases are most likely at work? anchoring and confirmation bias the halo effect and social loafing stereotype threat and altruism the mere exposure effect only

a patient's family expects to make medical decisions together. ana says, 'our way, where each patient decides alone, is the only proper way.' ben says, 'their way is far more advanced than ours.' cara says, 'that makes sense given how much their culture values family.' who is practicing cultural relativism? cara only ana only ben only ben and cara

after a nurse snaps at a patient, four coworkers explain why. which explanation is a dispositional attribution? 'she's just an impatient person by nature.' 'the unit was badly understaffed today.' 'the patient had been rude to her first.' 'it was the end of a 15 hour double shift.'

a hiring manager learns that an applicant is 'very organized' and assumes he is also punctual and detail oriented, but makes no assumption about whether he is friendly. why does this fit implicit personality theory better than the halo effect? he links specific traits he believes go together, not a general glow he judges the applicant entirely positively based on one good trait he attributes the applicant's organization to the situation, not traits he expects the applicant to confirm a stereotype about his social group

staff at one hospital describe their own team as full of different personalities, but say the staff at a rival hospital are "all the same." this illustrates: the out group homogeneity effect the false consensus effect the halo effect for one's own team group polarization among staff

one group hears a person described as "intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious." another hears the same list in reverse order. the first group rates the person more favorably. this shows: the primacy effect in impression formation the recency effect in impression formation the halo effect of physical attractiveness the false consensus effect

a manager has a positive view of a resident for months, but after one recent serious error, that error dominates her whole impression of him. this illustrates: the recency effect the primacy effect the halo effect the out group homogeneity effect

a student who skips most lectures estimates that 80% of classmates also skip, when the true figure is 20%. this illustrates: the false consensus effect the fundamental attribution error the optimism bias social loafing

most young adults in a survey say they are less likely than the average person their age to be hurt in a car crash. this is: optimism bias the false consensus effect the just world hypothesis hindsight bias

a family insists that imported products are always better than those made in their own country and looks down on local customs. this attitude is called: xenocentrism ethnocentrism cultural relativism assimilation

at a summer camp, two groups of boys grew hostile after contests in which only one group could win prizes. hostility dropped after the groups worked together on a series of shared goals, such as fixing the camp's water supply. the rise in hostility best supports: realistic conflict theory the just world hypothesis stereotype threat the mere exposure effect

during a recession, many residents blame a small immigrant community for job losses that were actually caused by factory automation. this best illustrates: scapegoating cultural relativism stereotype threat the out group homogeneity effect

neighbors begin avoiding the parents of a child with a highly stigmatized illness, even though the parents are healthy. erving goffman called this spread of disgrace to people linked to a stigmatized person: courtesy stigma master status labeling stereotype threat

a landlord refuses to rent to applicants of one religion, even though city laws and policies forbid it. this is an example of: individual discrimination institutional discrimination prejudice without discrimination stereotype threat

after hearing that a stranger was robbed while walking home at night, several people say, "she should have known better." which belief most likely drives this reaction? the just world hypothesis the out group homogeneity effect cultural relativism the primacy effect

before a guest lecture, half a class read that the speaker was "rather warm" and half that he was "rather cold"; the rest of the description was identical. after the same lecture, the 'warm' group rated him as more considerate and sociable. this shows that: central traits strongly shape overall impressions recent information outweighs earlier information actual behavior overrides prior descriptions self serving bias distorts people's self ratings

older adults scored lower on a memory test when told it measured age related memory decline than when told it measured general learning. the best explanation is: stereotype threat self serving bias the fundamental attribution error belief perseverance

in a 'jigsaw' classroom, each student in a mixed ethnicity group learns one part of a lesson and must teach it to the others, because everyone is tested on the whole lesson. prejudice drops over time. the method works mainly through: cooperative interdependence toward a shared goal exposure alone, without any need to cooperate rewards for the single best student in each group teacher praise for the least prejudiced students

maria yells at a nurse. she also yells at other staff in other settings (low distinctiveness), has yelled at this nurse before (high consistency), and no one else yells at this nurse (low consensus). kelley's covariation model predicts observers will attribute her behavior to: maria's personality (an internal cause) the nurse's behavior (an external cause) temporary circumstances of that one day the hospital setting (a situational cause)

a person attributes an out group member's kind act to luck or a special situation, but attributes the same person's rude act to the 'nature' of their group. thomas pettigrew called this: the ultimate attribution error the actor observer bias in judging others the self serving bias the false consensus effect

men talked by phone with women they were told (at random) were attractive or unattractive. listeners who heard only the women's side of the call rated the 'attractive' women as warmer and friendlier. this best demonstrates: behavioral confirmation (a self fulfilling prophecy) a halo effect existing only in the men's minds stereotype threat felt by the women themselves the matching hypothesis of romantic attraction

rosenthal and jacobson told teachers that some randomly chosen students were about to 'bloom' intellectually. those students later showed larger iq gains. which explanation is best supported by later research? teachers gave them more warmth, attention and feedback those students truly had higher ability at the start those students worked harder after seeing their scores graders scored those students' tests more generously

participants were falsely told they were very good at telling real suicide notes from fake ones. even after learning the feedback was made up, they still believed they had above average skill. this is: belief perseverance hindsight bias the false consensus effect the primacy effect in memory

boys were sorted into groups by a trivial preference (which of two painters they liked) and never met their group members. when dividing rewards, many picked options that maximized the gap between groups, even when that gave their own group less overall. which theory best explains this? social identity theory realistic conflict theory kin selection theory social exchange theory

in the 1930s, a researcher toured the u.s. with a chinese couple and was refused service at only 1 of about 250 hotels and restaurants. months later, most places that answered a mailed letter said they would not serve chinese guests. what does this study most directly show? stated prejudice does not always predict discrimination discrimination always follows from stated prejudice institutional policies caused the in person refusals the couple's presence created stereotype threat

students read an essay praising fidel castro. some were told the writer chose that position freely; others were told a debate coach assigned it. even in the assigned condition, readers rated the writer as fairly pro castro. this finding best shows: the fundamental attribution error (correspondence bias) the actor observer bias, since readers were the actors the self serving bias in judging the writer's essay belief perseverance after the readers were debriefed

a clinic wants to reduce self stigma among patients with depression. which intervention targets self stigma most directly? group sessions helping patients challenge their own shame a media campaign to reduce the public's fear of mental illness new laws banning hiring discrimination against patients training employers to support workers with depression

adorno's f scale measured the authoritarian personality. every item was worded so that agreeing raised the authoritarianism score. why did critics see this as a problem? people who agree with most statements score high regardless of views authoritarian people refuse to complete any personality questionnaire the scale measured intelligence instead of attitudes toward authority agreement wording makes the scale too short to give reliable scores

goffman described three types of stigma. patient 1 has visible facial burn scars. patient 2 has a prison record. patient 3 belongs to a stigmatized religious minority, as did his parents. which classification is correct? body (1), character (2), tribal (3) tribal (1), body (2), character (3) character (1), tribal (2), body (3) body (1), tribal (2), character (3)

after failing an exam, student 1 says, 'i'm just not smart enough.' student 2 says, 'i didn't study enough.' according to weiner's attribution theory, which student is more likely to try harder next time, and why? student 2; effort is unstable and controllable student 1, because ability is internal and stable student 2, because effort is an external cause student 1, because ability is under one's control

the grid shows the stereotype content model (fiske, cuddy, glick and xu). which emotion belongs in the cell marked ? (groups seen as competent but cold, such as wealthy professionals)? envy pity contempt admiration

jim believes society works best when some groups stay on top and others stay at the bottom, and he opposes policies that promote equality between groups. this reflects high: social dominance orientation belief in a just world collectivist orientation cultural relativism

a medical student spills coffee on his white coat before rounds and is sure everyone noticed, but almost nobody did. overestimating how much others notice us is the: spotlight effect false consensus effect actor observer bias illusion of control

before working with a group of refugees, some volunteers feel tense and worry about saying the wrong thing, so they avoid contact. walter and cookie stephan called this: intergroup anxiety stereotype threat courtesy stigma intergroup scapegoating

a job applicant is polite and agreeable throughout an interview. according to correspondent inference theory (jones and davis), this tells observers little about her true personality mainly because: politeness is expected of anyone in that situation politeness is always caused by a stable inner trait interviews produce behavior with high distinctiveness observers can never make inferences about others

aggressive children who are bumped by a peer in an unclear situation are more likely than other children to assume it was done on purpose. kenneth dodge described this as: hostile attribution bias self serving attribution bias just world belief belief perseverance

coach ruiz shouted at a player during practice today. using the information in the table and kelley's covariation model, the most likely cause is: unusual circumstances today coach ruiz's irritable personality something about the player himself the team's rules on discipline

a student asks to borrow class notes. classmates are much more willing to help when he missed class because of an eye infection than when he went to the beach. weiner would explain the difference mainly by the: perceived controllability of the cause perceived stability of the cause student's internal locus of control low consensus of his behavior

in a 1974 study by langer and abelson, therapists watched the same videotaped interview of a young man. those told he was a 'patient' rated him as much more disturbed than those told he was a 'job applicant'. this best illustrates how: a label shapes how identical behavior is interpreted the man acted differently in the two versions of the tape therapists are always more accurate than untrained raters job applicants tend to hide their psychological problems

in a hypothetical study, managers with power over hiring spent less time reading details about each applicant and relied more on group stereotypes than coworkers with no say in hiring. this fits the idea that: power lowers the need to attend to individuals stereotypes are used only by low status people power makes social judgments more accurate more details always increase stereotyping

after two rival hospitals merge, leaders stress that everyone now belongs to one 'valley health' team, and bias between the former staff groups drops. this best illustrates: recategorization into a common in group realistic conflict over scarce resources the out group homogeneity effect scapegoating of the former rival

a runner who exercises every day believes that very few people her age exercise regularly, though most actually do. this is the: false uniqueness effect false consensus effect spotlight effect unrealistic optimism bias

white students who simply knew that a white friend had a close black friend reported less prejudice toward black people, even though they had no such friendships themselves. this is the: extended contact effect mere exposure effect jigsaw classroom effect superordinate goal effect

participants read statements describing acts by members of a large group 1 and a small group 2 (table; hypothetical). later, most overestimated how many undesirable acts group 2 members did. what best explains this? pairing two rare things makes them seem linked group 2 truly did a larger share of bad acts participants belonged to group 1 and disliked group 2 small groups are always seen as more desirable

black and white seventh graders wrote briefly about values important to them; a control group wrote about unimportant values. black students' grades improved, narrowing the racial gap, while white students' grades were unchanged. the best explanation is that the exercise: reduced threat by affirming the students' self worth taught study skills that raised every student's grades lowered teachers' expectations of the white students created stereotype threat for the white students only

residents' ratings of neighborhood disorder were predicted by the share of black and poor residents, even after controlling for disorder (litter, graffiti) recorded by trained observers. this suggests that: stereotypes about groups shape how places are perceived observers' recordings of disorder were not accurate residents perceive their surroundings without any bias at all racial makeup directly causes more physical disorder

in a survey, people who believe the public sees psychiatric patients as dangerous are less likely to seek therapy for their own symptoms, even when the symptoms are severe. this pattern is best described as: label avoidance driven by public stigma courtesy stigma from family members stereotype threat during treatment the belief in a just world

women told that a math test shows gender differences scored lower than women told it did not, and they also did worse on a working memory task given during the session. what does this suggest? threat uses up working memory needed for the test women naturally have less working memory than men the instructions only lowered the women's effort weak working memory is what causes the stereotypes

white participants who reported low prejudice reviewed job candidates whose qualifications were strong, ambiguous or weak (hypothetical data in the graph). which conclusion is best supported? bias appears when a decision can be justified on other grounds participants were biased against black candidates in every case ambiguous resumes lowered both candidates' ratings by the same amount the low prejudice participants showed no racial bias at all

physicians took an implicit association test and then read cases of patients with identical heart attack symptoms who differed only by race. doctors with stronger implicit pro white bias were less likely to recommend clot dissolving drugs for black patients, although self reported bias was low and did not predict decisions. which conclusion is best supported? implicit bias predicted decisions that self reports missed explicit attitudes are the best predictor of care black patients need clot dissolving drugs less often the doctors were consciously hiding their true racial views

white participants did worse on a golf task when it was described as measuring 'natural athletic ability', while black participants did worse when it was described as measuring 'sports intelligence'. what does this show about stereotype threat? any group can be affected when a relevant stereotype is made salient it only affects groups that have low social status in society black athletes truly have less sports intelligence than white athletes telling people a task's purpose always lowers their scores

which of the following are examples of discrimination rather than only a stereotype or prejudice? i. a manager declines to interview applicants with foreign sounding names. ii. a man believes that older adults are bad with technology. iii. a landlord feels uneasy around tenants of a different religion. i only ii only i and iii only i, ii and iii

researchers want to (1) estimate how strongly u.s. adults endorse belief in a just world and (2) test whether reading a news story about an assault victim increases victim blaming. which statements about their methods are correct? i. randomly sampling participants from all u.s. adults would improve the external validity of the estimate in aim 1. ii. randomly assigning participants to read the assault story or a neutral story would support a causal conclusion for aim 2. iii. random assignment alone would ensure that results for aim 2 apply to all u.s. adults. i only i and ii only ii and iii only i, ii and iii

a driver who is cut off on the highway immediately thinks, “what a selfish jerk,” without considering that the other driver might be rushing to a hospital. this illustrates: the fundamental attribution error the self serving bias the just world hypothesis the false consensus effect

a medical student says she failed her anatomy exam because it was unfair and she had a cold, but says her classmate failed because he is lazy. her explanations best illustrate: the halo effect the actor observer bias a self fulfilling prophecy the mere exposure effect

students rated how much each of several causes explained their grade on a recent exam. among students with high grades, 78% chose “my ability or effort” as the main cause and 12% chose “an easy test.” among students with low grades, 18% chose “my ability or effort” and 64% chose “an unfair or hard test.” these data best illustrate: the false consensus effect the fundamental attribution error the self serving bias the just world hypothesis

everyone in a theater laughs at a comedian (high consensus). maya laughs at this comedian but rarely at other comedians (high distinctiveness), and she laughs every time she sees him (high consistency). according to kelley’s covariation model, maya’s laughter will most likely be attributed to: the comedian, an external cause maya’s personality, an internal cause chance circumstances on one night maya’s mood on that particular day

a nurse who smokes knows that smoking causes cancer. according to cognitive dissonance theory, which response would reduce her discomfort without changing her behavior? fully accepting that smoking is harmful while continuing to smoke as before quitting smoking with the help of nicotine patches deciding that the health risks of smoking are exaggerated for people like her increasing the number of cigarettes she smokes each day

students who went through a difficult, embarrassing initiation to join a study club rate the club’s dull meetings as more valuable than students who joined with no initiation. this best illustrates: the mere exposure effect effort justification, a form of dissonance reduction social loafing the foot in the door technique used by club officers

burn these pages

what the trash remembers

the author's main purpose in the passage is to: argue that discarded material is a valuable source that is nonetheless filtered by preservation and interpretation show that written records are a much more trustworthy guide to the past than the objects that people simply threw away explain the methods archaeologists use to date pottery, bones and tools recovered from refuse heaps prove that ancient societies were wealthier than their surviving trash suggests in nearly every case
