the author mentions studies of modern household garbage in order to: support the claim that discarded material can contradict what people say about their own habits show that modern families waste far more food than the ancient households that archaeologists study illustrate how quickly cloth, wood and most foods decay once they have been thrown away suggest that archaeologists should study modern trash instead of ancient refuse heaps

according to the author, what is the central error in claiming that trash is an unbiased record? it assumes that a record no one meant to shape has not been shaped it assumes that the people who wrote chronicles and letters were always deliberately dishonest it assumes that archaeologists can excavate all kinds of refuse heaps with equal ease it assumes that ordinary households threw away more than courts, temples and trading houses

archaeologists excavate a very dry desert cave where baskets, textiles and wooden bowls have survived alongside pottery. based on the passage, the author would most likely expect this site to: give a fuller picture of people's possessions than sites where only pottery and stone survive provide an unfiltered record of daily life that requires no interpretation at all by archaeologists show that the people who lived there were poorer and simpler than their neighbors elsewhere be less useful than nearby written records because perishable goods are hard to interpret

researchers studying an ancient town find many stone tools and pottery shards but almost no textiles. based on the passage, they should be cautious about concluding that: the town's people rarely made or used cloth. the town existed and was occupied by people for some period. pottery was made, used or traded there at some point. stone tools survive well in the soil around the town.

the comparison at the end of the passage, between the archaeologist and the historian who believes a royal chronicle, serves to: show that both commit the same error of trusting a source without examining its biases. prove that royal chronicles are more reliable than objects. argue that archaeology is useless as a guide to the past. show that historians and archaeologists have long disliked and distrusted each other's work.
ten cents a bottle

which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage? small, certain rewards for returning containers can curb littering where rarely enforced fines fail littering fines should be raised until the expected cost of tossing a bottle becomes very large deposit systems succeed mainly because they persuade careless drivers to change their littering habits deposit systems unfairly burden the poor and should be replaced by expanded curbside recycling

in context, the phrase 'converts the indifference of some people into income for others' means that: containers some people discard carelessly become a source of earnings for those who collect them people who litter are eventually paid back the deposits they lost by throwing containers away bottlers profit from the deposits that careless customers never bother to reclaim from stores governments tax indifferent consumers in order to fund the wages of the poorly paid street cleaners

how does the author respond to the criticisms raised in paragraph 4? they are valid but call for improving deposit systems, not ending them they are mistaken, because collectors earn good wages from the containers they return they are decisive, showing that deposit systems do more harm than good on balance they are irrelevant, since the author cares only about how roadsides look to drivers

the claim in paragraph 1 that littering fines change little relies on which assumption? would be offenders consider the odds of detection, not only the penalty most people who litter do not know that littering is against the law cities would enforce littering laws strictly if they had enough money to do so fines for littering are too small to matter even on the rare occasions they are imposed

based on the passage, for which problem would the author most likely consider a deposit style reward appropriate? shoppers leaving carts around a parking lot, addressed by a coin deposit returned when a cart is put back illegal dumping of toxic waste, addressed by paying the factories that dump it a small bonus for proper disposal speeding on highways, addressed by doubling fines while keeping enforcement at current levels volunteering at shelters, addressed by paying a small fee to people who already help out of duty

given the reasoning of paragraph 3, which proposed reform of deposit systems would the author most likely oppose? refunding deposits only to original buyers who can show a receipt sending unclaimed deposits to a public fund for roadside cleanup having large stores install machines that sort returned empties opening return centers in poor areas with convenient opening hours

which finding would most strengthen the author's ‘broader lesson’ in paragraph 5? a town paying a small, sure sum per used syringe turned in recovered far more than one using seldom applied penalties. studies show that many people continue to litter even where trash cans and recycling bins are easy to find and free to use. most beverage bottles and cans sold today are made of glass, plastic or aluminum. some cities set very large fines for littering, sometimes hundreds of dollars per offense.
the tip jar's hidden job

which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage? tipping endures mainly because it eases an awkward social relationship, not because it rewards good service tipping should be abolished because it allows customers' moods and prejudices to determine workers' pay tipping works well because it lets the diners who are best placed to judge service reward it directly and fairly restaurants that replace tips with higher menu prices tend to earn more and keep their staff longer

the author mentions the smiling face drawn on the bill primarily in order to: show that gratuities hinge on signals unrelated to how well diners were served recommend a practical technique that servers can use to increase their earnings prove that diners deliberately punish servers who are slow, careless or make mistakes illustrate how customers express gratitude in societies that profess equality

what role does paragraph 4 play in the passage? it supplies support for the social account over the economic one it introduces the main objection to the social explanation that the author goes on to reject it shows that customers paid far more once tipping was replaced by higher prices it describes how restaurants first adopted tipping as a substitute for wages

the author's view of reformers who want to abolish tipping is best described as: sympathetic to their concern for workers but doubtful that a wage fix alone will work dismissive, because the author believes tipping causes workers no real harm fully supportive, because the author sees tipping purely as a problem of wages hostile, because the author believes reformers secretly serve the interests of restaurant owners

based on the passage, which no tipping policy would the author expect to have the best chance of lasting? higher menu prices plus a card on which diners can write a personal thanks to their server higher menu prices with a printed notice on each menu explaining that service is already included lower menu prices paired with a fixed service charge added automatically to each bill unchanged menu prices, with servers paid a bonus based on table turnover

which finding would most strengthen the author's social explanation of tipping? diners in no tip nations feel more uneasy about being waited on than diners where gratuities are the norm. studies show that tip amounts generally track the size of the bill rather than the quality of service received. surveys show that most servers would prefer higher, steadier wages to tips. some well known restaurants have abolished tipping and raised menu prices instead.

the author's conclusion from the restaurants that restored tipping would be most weakened if it were found that: servers left mainly over lower pay, and diners did not miss tipping customers paid about the same total under the new pricing as before some diners at the no tip restaurants still tried to leave cash for staff the restaurants were all located in countries where tipping is customary
counting by the household

the central claim of the passage is that: household surveys are useful but can hide unequal conditions among people who live together household surveys should be replaced by surveys that interview each person in a household separately poverty statistics are unreliable because people misreport their incomes to interviewers families usually divide their resources fairly according to each member's real needs

the primary purpose of paragraph 2 is to: concede that treating the household as a unit is often sensible show that most children in poor households have no income argue that teenagers with jobs should be counted as separate households explain why household surveys are cheaper than other methods

which household would the standard household method be most likely to misdescribe? one above the poverty line whose disabled son gets no share of its spending one of three adults who each earn a similar wage and divide all of their costs evenly one below the poverty line in which every member goes without to roughly the same degree one in which a teenager with no earnings lives with two well paid parents who provide for her

the author mentions estimates of unpaid housework and illegal markets in order to: undercut the claim that inequality within households is too hard to measure show that household surveys already capture most forms of hidden or unreported income suggest that unpaid housework is the main cause of poverty within families argue that governments should treat family finances as a private matter

a national survey reports that average household income in a region rose sharply over a decade. based on the passage, the author would most likely caution that: some individuals in those homes may have seen no real improvement in their lives the rise must reflect errors made by the survey's interviewers poverty in the region has probably increased over the same period individual incomes in the region are likely to have risen even faster

a program pays a child benefit to each household's main earner. later studies that measure individuals find that the children's nutrition barely improved, though household income rose. which explanation fits the passage best? the money went to whoever controlled spending, not necessarily to the children. household surveys overstated how much each household's income had really risen. the benefit was too small to make a difference to the household's average income. children's diets are a private family matter that such studies cannot measure.

which reasoning makes the same error the author identifies when saying cost is 'a reason for economy, not a proof of accuracy'? a city keeps one traffic sensor per district to save money, then treats each figure as exact for every street. a city puts a costly sensor on every street even though rough district averages would meet its needs. a city places one traffic sensor per district to save money and reports the figures as rough averages for each district. a city stops counting traffic altogether because a sensor on every street would cost more than its budget allows.
cash in the wake of a storm

which statement best captures the main idea of the passage? money transfers frequently outperform supplies, yet their value hinges on the setting aid agencies should return to shipping goods, since cash raises prices for survivors cash aid works best because it lets survivors avoid the indignity of waiting in line disaster aid fails mainly because donors send goods that survivors do not need

the author's remark that families 'converted goods into cash anyway, only less efficiently' is used to suggest that: survivors' own choices showed that cash was the more useful aid in kind aid failed mostly because agencies shipped the wrong amounts survivors who sold their kits were exploiting the relief system markets after disasters usually work well enough for cash to succeed

the author's attitude toward the shift from goods to cash is best described as: approving overall, yet wary of money as a cure all strongly opposed, because cash weakens whole communities entirely uncritical, because cash is always cheaper indifferent, since both forms of aid fail equally

the concern raised in paragraph 4 differs from the concern in paragraph 3 in that it: points to a social cost of cash rather than a problem with markets shows that cash aid costs agencies more to deliver than shipments of goods argues that public lines for aid are a harm that should be avoided applies only in the first days after a disaster, before shops open

three weeks after an earthquake, a town's shops have reopened and are well stocked, but many families have lost their incomes. based on the passage, the author would most likely recommend: handing affected households money to use at the reopened stores trucking in food and tents, since aid in goods is more visible holding back all aid until families have found new sources of income paying shop owners directly so they can lower prices for everyone

which finding would most strengthen the concern in paragraph 4? after an agency switched from public distribution to phone transfers, fewer survivors learned which roads and clinics had reopened. audits show that cash transfers are much cheaper for agencies to deliver than trucked in goods. surveys show that most survivors prefer choosing their own goods with cash over receiving standard kits of donated supplies by truck. market data show that local prices for food and fuel rose sharply in the weeks after a flood.

applying the question the author says agencies should ask, which situation most clearly calls for goods rather than cash? a district whose shops reopened but get no deliveries since its bridge fell; prices have tripled a farming region where shipped food aid would arrive just as local farmers are bringing in a harvest a suburb with open, well stocked shops where survivors dislike queuing in public for supplies a town where families sold half of their standard aid kits at a loss to buy other things they needed

in the final paragraph, 'the old mistake' that treating cash as the answer everywhere would repeat is best understood as: applying one form of aid to crises whose conditions differ leaving donated clothing to rot unsorted in distant warehouses sending money into towns where the shops have nothing to sell ignoring survivors' stated preferences about the aid they get
what a street is called

the author's main argument is that: street names confer public honor, so the fairness of how they are chosen matters most streets named for disgraced figures should be renamed quickly and without lengthy public debate renaming streets erases history and should be avoided except after a revolution street names are a poor way of teaching residents about their city's history

the primary function of paragraph 2 is to: grant a reasonable point to opponents of renaming before challenging them show that most cities revise their street names every generation explain why new governments rename so many streets soon after taking power argue that street signs are the best record of a city's history

the author's observation that few residents know much about the person their street commemorates supports the claim that: naming a road serves to pay tribute more than to teach the past residents should be taught more about the history of their streets renaming a street will confuse residents and visitors who use maps old names should be preserved because so few people remember them

the author's claim that keeping a street's name is 'not the neutral act its defenders imply' would be most weakened if it were shown that: most street names arose from long informal use, not from any official decision most residents use their street's name only as an address and nothing more some streets have changed names several times without any claim of lost history renamings imposed overnight by new governments are often reversed later on

a city council, meeting late at night without public notice, votes to rename a major avenue after a popular local activist. based on the passage, the author would most likely predict that: the renaming may provoke bitterness and eventually be undone the new name will be accepted because the activist is popular residents will soon forget the avenue's old name and its history the decision will settle the city's naming debates for good

which finding would most strengthen the author's argument in paragraph 5? road names picked via open community consultation were undone more rarely than those dictated by new regimes. city records show that many street signs must be replaced each year because of theft, vandalism and ordinary wear. surveys show residents rarely know who their street is named for or why. some streets in older cities have changed names several times over two centuries.

the author's distinction between ‘remembering and honoring’ (paragraph 3) is used to argue that: changing a name does not erase history, which is recorded elsewhere. street names are the main way that most people learn their local history. all names honoring controversial figures should be changed. history books are less reliable than street names as records.
the pension and the family

which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage? pensions reduce cash from children to parents, but family support overall need not decline public pensions weaken families by replacing a bond of duty with a bureaucratic monthly check public pensions strengthen every form of support that adult children give their parents adult children send less money to parents mainly because of the quarrels it causes

which finding would most weaken the author's argument in paragraph 3? after pensions expanded, the time children spent caring for parents fell as sharply as the cash they sent after pensions expanded, more elderly people chose to live in their own homes instead of with their adult children or other relatives after pensions expanded, elderly people reported fewer quarrels with their children about money after pensions expanded, adult children in distant cities sent less cash home to their parents

a study finds that after a pension expansion, adult children sent less money home; visits fell among children living in distant cities but held steady among those living nearby. the author would most likely interpret this as: the pattern the author's caveat about migrated children leads one to expect proof of the crowding out worry, since total family support plainly declined a refutation of the view that time spent helping parents stays level or rises evidence that migration, not pensions, caused the drop in money sent home

the limits described in paragraph 4 serve mainly to: temper the optimism by noting where such payments could erode caregiving. reject the author's whole argument about the effects of pensions on families. prove that pensions harm families wherever they are introduced. show that migration of adult children is rare in such places.
whose park is it?

which statement best captures the main idea of the passage? early urban parks largely fulfilled their promise of bringing the classes together as equals. early urban parks were instruments of social control for the wealthy and the powerful, and nothing more than that. because new parks raise nearby rents and push out residents, cities should stop building them. though early parks reflected class based aims, their democratic promise gave residents leverage to reshape them.

the author's attitude toward the historians described in the first paragraph is best described as: agreement with their evidence but disagreement with their conclusion. complete rejection of both their evidence and their reasoning. full endorsement of their view that park rhetoric was mere ideology. indifference, since historical debates have no bearing on present parks.

the author's reply to the skeptic in paragraph 4 depends on the assumption that: streets and squares were never the site of struggles over public use. a place's official mission can shape which claims its users are able to make. commissioners eventually adopted residents' views willingly and without pressure. petitioning was the only method that working class residents ever used to change their city's parks.

the author's description of picnics that the commissioners ‘had not imagined and did not approve’ supports the claim that: the grounds' eventual uses went beyond their designers' plans. parks were rarely used by working families on their days off. commissioners largely succeeded in controlling how visitors behaved. working people disliked parks and preferred streets and squares.
the arithmetic of dread

the central claim of the passage is that: the public is generally better than experts at judging which risks are really worth worrying about. lay views of danger at odds with specialists' data may reflect true priorities, not mistakes. experts should stop presenting probabilities and statistics to the public altogether. public misjudgments of risk are caused mainly by news coverage.

the author refers to optical illusions primarily in order to: argue that evidence of some errors does not show that all differing judgments are errors. concede that the public's perception of risk is fundamentally unreliable in most situations. explain that framing effects are a kind of visual perception problem. suggest that experts are just as subject to illusions as the public.

the example of the neighborhood downwind of a chemical plant is used mainly to support the claim that: chemical plants pose far greater dangers to the health of nearby residents than coal plants do. people overestimate unfamiliar risks, like chemical plants, far more than familiar ones like driving. people's worry may follow whether a hazard was agreed to and fairly shared, not merely its odds. regulators should shut down industrial plants that operate close to residential neighborhoods.

residents oppose a planned waste incinerator, though experts calculate that it would raise local cancer risk only slightly. the residents point out that they were never consulted and that the facility mainly serves a wealthier town nearby. based on the passage, the author would most likely recommend that regulators: keep explaining the small risk figures, more clearly each time, until the residents' opposition fades. respond to residents' concerns about consent and fairness, not only present risk estimates. dismiss the opposition as an example of framing bias that experts have already documented. cancel the incinerator, since public fear should decide such questions.

a regulator explains a new pipeline's risks using only expected deaths per year, and residents remain opposed because they were never consulted. based on the passage, the author would most likely say that: the opponents may be protesting a lack of say, which no calculation can resolve. the residents are simply bad at math and need the numbers explained again. the regulator should present more numbers, such as injuries as well as deaths. the pipeline must be cancelled, since the residents' fears should decide the matter in the end.

as used in paragraph 2, “crowd out” most nearly means: fill a donation center beyond its capacity on busy days. displace a motive that would otherwise have led people to act. attract donors who are in financial distress and need money. reduce the safety of the blood supply by adding risky or unhealthy donors.

which claim does the author present as having become less persuasive over time? paid donors pose a much greater risk of passing on infections. blood is part of the body and should not be treated as a commodity. countries with blood shortages may postpone surgeries. how an incentive is framed affects how donors respond.

the author would most likely agree that a wealthy country that relies on plasma bought from paid donors abroad should: ban the purchase of plasma from abroad immediately, whatever the resulting shortage at home. start paying all of its own blood donors so it no longer needs imports. stop collecting blood from volunteers and rely on paid donors instead. examine whether its policies match the moral claims it makes for its unpaid system.
the problem with finding more

which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage? screening programs should be abandoned because, on balance, they cause far more harm than good to the patients they test. testing can hurt people by catching harmless irregularities, so its worth lies in lives saved, not cases found. most of the cancers that screening programs find are actually false positives caused by test errors. five year survival is the best measure of whether a screening program is actually working for patients.

the author discusses five year survival rates (paragraph 4) primarily in order to: show that screening has greatly increased how long patients live after their diagnosis. explain why a commonly cited measure can make screening look helpful when it is not. argue that doctors should stop collecting survival statistics. show that tumors found early by screening always shrink on their own without treatment.

based on the passage, which pattern would be the strongest sign that a screening program is mainly finding dangerous cancers earlier? diagnoses rise sharply and stay high, while deaths remain unchanged. five year survival among diagnosed patients doubles. new diagnoses climb then taper off, and mortality falls patients report more anxiety after screening begins.

after a new thyroid screening test is introduced, diagnoses in a region triple over 15 years, five year survival rises from 80% to 97%, and the death rate from the disease does not change. based on the passage, the most reasonable conclusion is that: the program has saved many lives, as the much higher survival rate clearly shows. the program has likely produced substantial overdiagnosis without reducing deaths. the new test produces a large number of false positives that are counted as cancers. thyroid disease has become far more common in the region.

which new finding would most strengthen the author's argument? patients whose cancers are found by screening say they feel relieved to know and are grateful that they had the test. screening tests have become much better at telling real abnormalities apart from simple test errors. treatments for advanced cancers have improved over the past decade. autopsies of people who died of other causes find small, untreated tumors of the screened type in many of them.

according to paragraph 3, overdiagnosis is "hard to see in individual cases" because: no one can tell whether a given treated tumor would ever have caused harm. pathologists often mistake normal tissue for cancer when they examine a sample. figures on diagnoses and deaths are seldom gathered for whole populations. patients who are treated after screening rarely report the harms they suffer.

which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that deliberation turns assembly members into “something else” than a sample of the public? assembly members were far more representative in age, income, education and occupation than the elected legislators were. in a number of such panels, participants' end of process opinions mirrored contemporaneous polls of the population. members said that expert testimony was the most useful and most trusted part of the whole process. some assemblies recommended policies that legislators later rejected or ignored.

which of the following is most similar to the author's view of what a citizens' assembly's recommendation represents? a random opinion poll of voters taken on election day, reported in the news as the public's settled view a campaign speech by a candidate who is seeking reelection and wants voters' support a public referendum in which each eligible citizen may vote on the same question advice from patients who studied a hospital policy for weeks with expert help: useful, but not a survey

in the final paragraph, the "more modest" promise that the author attributes to the lottery's modern form is that: ordinary people picked at random can reason carefully when given the chance. every citizen has an equal chance of being chosen to hold a governing office. randomly chosen panels will arrive at the views that the wider public holds. assembly members will steer elected legislators toward more moderate policy.
when memory is the evidence

which of the following best states the main idea of the passage? written documents are more reliable than oral testimony, so documents should win whenever the two disagree. errors in oral testimony are usually the most revealing evidence a historian has about a community's beliefs and its values. both oral testimony and documents are shaped by their makers' purposes, so each must be interpreted, not simply trusted. oral history became respected only after its practitioners proved that ordinary memory was accurate.

the author's attitude toward historians who treat “the errors themselves as evidence” is best described as: appreciative but cautious. dismissive and very impatient. uncritically enthusiastic. neutral and uninterested.
